passage: Madhav ran a small agricultural supply shop in a town near Hubli. His phone buzzed all day with group chats, videos and news alerts. One evening he realised he'd spent two hours watching short clips and forgotten to call a farmer back about seeds. His friend Eshaan, a schoolteacher, had deleted most apps from his own phone. "I kept only what I need," Eshaan said. "Business chat, bank, weather." Madhav tried it. He muted twenty groups, deleted the video app and put his phone in a drawer after nine. The first week felt restless; he kept reaching for it. By the third week he'd read half a book on soil health. Business calls got returned the same day.

qa.q: How long had Madhav spent watching short clips that evening?
qa.a: He had spent two hours watching them.

qa.q: What does Madhav keep reaching for his phone in the first week suggest?
qa.a: It suggests his habit was strong and he felt restless without constant updates.

qa.q: What made Madhav's changes effective?
qa.a: He removed apps he didn't need, muted distracting groups and set a time for the phone to go away.

qa.q: How might the farmers Madhav works with see this change?
qa.a: They'd likely notice he calls back faster and seems more attentive, which builds trust. 🙂

grounding: Shows a young shopkeeper choosing his technology deliberately instead of by default.

passage: Kaito, a graphic designer in Osaka, noticed he checked the news every time he waited for a file to render. He felt anxious and scattered by lunchtime. His colleague Nadia had a different system: she read one weekly news summary on Sunday and nothing else. "Isn't that out of touch?" Kaito asked. "I miss nothing important," she said. "Important things are still there on Sunday." Kaito tried a milder version. He removed news apps, kept one trusted source he read in the evening, and set his phone to grayscale during work. The first days he felt left out of office chatter. After a month, he found he could hold a design idea in his head for an hour without losing it.

qa.q: When does Nadia read her weekly news summary?
qa.a: She reads it on Sunday.

qa.q: How did Kaito feel before changing his habits?
qa.a: He felt anxious and scattered by lunchtime from checking news constantly.

qa.q: What choices did Kaito make to use technology more deliberately?
qa.a: He removed news apps, kept one trusted source for evenings and set his phone to grayscale at work.

qa.q: How does Nadia see keeping up with the news?
qa.a: She believes important news will still be there on Sunday, so constant checking isn't necessary.

grounding: Shows a young designer choosing his information diet consciously after seeing a colleague's approach.

passage: At the engineering firm's weekly team meeting, Vaibhav noticed everyone, including himself, was typing on laptops while someone presented. Nobody remembered decisions afterward. As the newest team lead, he proposed an experiment: laptops closed in meetings except for the note-taker, and messages answered in two batches a day instead of instantly. Akash, the senior engineer, scoffed. "Clients expect quick replies." "Urgent calls still come through," Vaibhav said. "Let's try two weeks." The first week was awkward; people fidgeted. By the second, meetings ended fifteen minutes early. Akash admitted he'd finished a design he'd been stuck on for a month. He didn't say thanks. But he started closing his laptop without being asked.

qa.q: How often would messages be answered in Vaibhav's experiment?
qa.a: They would be answered in two batches a day.

qa.q: Why did Akash scoff at the proposal at first?
qa.a: He worried that clients would be unhappy if replies weren't quick.

qa.q: What made Vaibhav's experiment easier for the team to accept?
qa.a: He framed it as a short two-week trial and kept urgent calls open, so people didn't feel cut off.

qa.q: How did Akash's view seem to change?
qa.a: After finishing a stuck design, he quietly began closing his laptop in meetings, showing he saw the benefit.

grounding: Shows a young team lead introducing deliberate tech habits at work and colleagues slowly adopting them.

passage:
Dear Bhavna,
You asked what happened with my 'phone experiment', so here's the full report. In September I noticed I picked up my phone about a hundred times a day, mostly without deciding to. So I did an audit: I listed every app and asked, 'Did I choose this, or did it choose me?' I kept maps, banking, messages, my music and the reading app. Deleted the rest, including two social apps I'd had since college. I moved email to the laptop only, checked twice a day. On weekends I use Nani's old keypad phone. The first week I kept reaching for a phone that wasn't there, honestly twitchy. By week three I'd finished two novels and restarted my sketchbook. I haven't become a monk. I still watch shows, but I choose them now. Want to try it with me in November?
Love,
Minakshi

qa.q: What question did Minakshi ask about each app?
qa.a: 'Did I choose this, or did it choose me?'

qa.q: How did Minakshi feel in the first week, and what does it show?
qa.a: Twitchy and restless, reaching for a phone that was not there, which shows how automatic the habit had become.

qa.q: Which of Minakshi's choices made that technology use more deliberate?
qa.a: Auditing the apps, deleting ones not really chosen, moving email to the laptop at set times, and using a keypad phone on weekends.

qa.q: How might Bhavna react to the invitation to try it in November?
qa.a: Probably curious, since Minakshi's results were real but balanced rather than preachy 😊

grounding: A letter shows a young adult auditing their apps and choosing tools and information diet deliberately.

passage: 'Abhinav bhai, how do you leave work so calm?' Irfan, the short version? I used to have eleven tools open at work and felt busy all day without finishing anything. Chat, email, three project boards, news tabs. One evening I realised I couldn't name a single thing I'd done that day that mattered. So I started choosing on purpose. I asked my team if we could agree on one place for tasks instead of three. That took a meeting and some grumbling, but we did it. I turned off all notifications except direct messages from my manager and two teammates. News I now read once, at lunch, from two sources I picked, not from whatever the feed pushes. And my phone stays in my bag during deep-work blocks. Honestly, the hardest part was the fear of missing something. I've missed almost nothing. And I leave work with a quieter head.

qa.q: How many tools did Abhinav used to have open at work?
qa.a: Eleven.

qa.q: What was the hardest part for Abhinav, and what does it show?
qa.a: The fear of missing something, which shows how closely his default tech habits were tied to anxiety.

qa.q: What changes made Abhinav's technology use deliberate?
qa.a: Agreeing on one task tool, limiting notifications to key people, reading news at lunch from chosen sources, and keeping his phone away during deep work.

qa.q: How might Abhinav's team have felt about switching to one task tool?
qa.a: Some grumbled at first, but they probably benefit from less scattered work too.

grounding: A young professional describes consciously choosing his work tools and information sources instead of living by default.
